name: Bistre Brown
lede: Bistre is a transparent brown made from wood soot, used for pen-and-ink washes and for glazing shadows in oil.

sections.title: Soot from a beech fire
sections.body:
Bistre was made from the soot of burnt wood, preferably beechwood [1]. The soot was collected close to the flames and treated with hot or boiling water. Once the particles had settled, the liquid was decanted and the sediment dried [1]. Coles describes it as a dark, transparent brown, a mixture of flame carbon, charred wood and tarry material that had not fully burned [3]. Ball adds that birch bark could serve in place of beech [4].

The name "bistre brown" is a variant of the plain name, which Paterson defines as the brown wash used in pen and ink drawings [2].

sections.title: Manuscripts, drawings and glazes
sections.body: Coles places its first use in 14th-century manuscript illumination, with wash drawings following in the 17th and 18th centuries [3]. Ball puts the earliest use at least as far back as the fourteenth century and notes that oil painters needed skill to get much from it [4]. Van Dyck glazed his shadows with it, as in his double portrait of the Stuart brothers of 1638-9 [4]. Paterson says it was later superseded by [[sepia]] [2]. For its neighbors in the earth browns, see [[umber]], [[raw-umber]] and [[brown]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a dark olive brown, nearest the ISCC-NBS name "light olive brown" at a distance of 2.2 [5]. It appears in 627 of our 23,781 paintings, 2.64 percent, as photographed [6]. That makes it more common than 80 percent of named colors, and it peaks in the 1400s, found in 22 of the 945 paintings from that century [6].
